questions.text: I consistently ask questions in board discussions that challenge the strategic assumptions underlying management's proposals.
I am able to identify strategic risks that management has not surfaced — and I raise them.
I distinguish between my role as a board member (governing strategy) and the executive's role (creating strategy), and I hold that boundary clearly.
I find that I tend to ratify management's strategic proposals rather than challenging their underlying logic. [R]
I bring a point of view to strategic board discussions that adds genuine value — not just process compliance or broad agreement.
I can evaluate strategic options at board level with genuine analytical independence, rather than relying entirely on management's framing.
I apply my fiduciary responsibilities with consistent rigour, even when it creates tension with management.
I can identify when a governance risk has reached the threshold requiring board escalation — and I act on that judgment.
I hold management accountable for their commitments in a way that is clear and consistent without undermining their authority to operate.
I sometimes defer to the dominant voice in the boardroom rather than pressing a governance concern I believe is valid. [R]
I understand the specific fiduciary and regulatory obligations that apply to my board role in the markets I operate in.
I can distinguish between governance risk and operational risk — and I engage at the governance level without overreaching into operations.
I have a clear and current map of the key stakeholders my board mandate requires me to understand and engage.
I navigate the dynamics between independent directors and management with deliberate intelligence — I understand where the power sits and how to engage it effectively.
In APAC governance contexts, I am comfortable operating in environments where government or political stakeholders have a direct relationship with the board.
I find APAC government-board stakeholder dynamics more difficult to navigate than investor or management stakeholders. [R]
I understand how major shareholder dynamics — including controlling family or state shareholders — affect board decision-making in the markets I operate in.
I bring useful stakeholder intelligence into board discussions — insights about investors, regulators, or market dynamics that strengthen the board's collective picture.
I think explicitly about the long-term legacy this board's decisions will create — not just the near-term performance metrics.
I advocate for decisions that protect the organisation's long-term health, even when they create short-term costs or discomfort.
I am more focused on the organisation's current performance metrics than on the lasting value the board is building. [R]
I think carefully about what institutional knowledge, governance standards, and values I am contributing to this organisation's enduring capability.
I consider what the board's track record will look like in 10 years — and I make governance decisions with that perspective in mind.
I push back when I believe a decision optimises for short-term optics at the expense of long-term institutional credibility.
My board or advisory profile — including my experience, network, and governance background — creates genuine credibility with APAC-native stakeholders.
I understand the governance and regulatory expectations of the specific APAC markets my board role requires me to engage (e.g., MAS in Singapore, CSRC/CAC in China, TSE reform standards in Japan).
I have been able to build or access the APAC relationships needed to carry my board mandate effectively in the markets that matter.
When I am in a room with senior APAC business leaders, government officials, or regulators, I can tell that my authority does not fully land in the way I would like it to. [R]
I understand the cultural norms — around consensus, hierarchy, face-saving, and relationship-first communication — that shape governance conversations in APAC board contexts.
My APAC governance credibility is actively strengthening — I am investing in the relationships, experience, and market intelligence that will deepen it over time.

archetypes.name: The Architect
archetypes.core_dynamic: Sets the standards and sees the big picture. The board member every chair wants. Rare combination of governance rigour and strategic intelligence operating at full strength.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: May become the dominant voice — suppressing other directors' contributions. Board monoculture risk.
archetypes.development_priority: Board chair succession readiness; sponsoring governance uplift in co-directors
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: If APAC Mandate Credibility <50, Architect profile may not translate to APAC-native boards — high Western credibility, APAC gap possible

archetypes.name: The Steward
archetypes.core_dynamic: Protects what has been built while building for the future. The institutional memory keeper. Brings a long-term governance lens that most boards undervalue.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: May resist necessary change. Over-conservatism can slow board adaptation to market shifts.
archetypes.development_priority: Innovation mindset development; engaging constructively with disruption
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: Strong in Japan and Singapore governance contexts; may have less traction in higher-velocity APAC markets (e.g., SE Asia startups, China state contexts)

archetypes.name: The Networker
archetypes.core_dynamic: Connects dots across stakeholders, surfaces opportunities, reads the boardroom dynamics with exceptional precision.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Governance depth may lag relationship breadth. Substance must match style.
archetypes.development_priority: Deepening governance rigour; building analytical independence to match stakeholder intelligence
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: APAC Networkers with government stakeholder relationships are highly valuable — this archetype's APAC Mandate Credibility score is the most important modifier

archetypes.name: The Guardian
archetypes.core_dynamic: Rigorous on process, consistent on fiduciary duties, but not yet contributing at full strategic level. The conscientious director.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Strategic contribution remains thin. May be seen as a procedural resource rather than a thought leader.
archetypes.development_priority: Strategic oversight development; learning to ask questions that reframe management's strategic proposals
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: Strong governance foundation makes this archetype credible across APAC markets — APAC Credibility gap most likely in market-specific intelligence

archetypes.name: The Visionary
archetypes.core_dynamic: Sees the future clearly. Brings genuine strategic intelligence. But governance mechanics are still tightening. Great strategist, developing director.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Governance gaps create risk exposure — may inadvertently overstep into executive territory.
archetypes.development_priority: Governance rigour; maintaining appropriate board/management boundary in strategic discussions
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: High value in APAC growth markets; may lack credibility with regulatory-facing boards (MAS, CSRC) where governance rigour is scrutinised

archetypes.name: The Bridge-Builder
archetypes.core_dynamic: Builds relationships and thinks long-term. A connector with a genuine commitment to lasting value. Growing governance capability.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Strategic oversight depth may be insufficient for complex board mandates.
archetypes.development_priority: Strategic oversight development; governance formalisation beyond process compliance
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: Strong APAC stakeholder relationship builder — often effective with APAC-native boards where relational credibility opens governance conversations

archetypes.name: The Nominee
archetypes.core_dynamic: Recently appointed or still developing governance capability. Potential is present — at least one dimension shows credible foundation.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Development stalls if not actively supported. Risk of becoming a Passenger if learning support is absent.
archetypes.development_priority: Structured board director development programme; mentorship pairing with experienced director
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: APAC-specific governance literacy development is highest priority — Western governance training alone is insufficient for APAC board contexts

archetypes.name: The Passenger
archetypes.core_dynamic: Attends meetings, votes with the majority, contributes minimally. The board member whose presence does not strengthen the board's collective capability.
archetypes.risk_if_unaddressed: Continued presence weakens board effectiveness and sets a governance floor that others adapt to.
archetypes.development_priority: Honest assessment conversation required: targeted development or board exit
archetypes.apac_modifier_note: APAC Mandate Credibility is likely very low — limited value in APAC governance contexts without fundamental capability development

archetypes.name: Axis 1
archetypes.description: Impact Orientation: How does the board member primarily create value? (Governance-dominant / Strategy-dominant / Relationship-dominant / Legacy-dominant / Balanced)

archetypes.name: Axis 2
archetypes.description: Mandate Strength Band: How credibly do they operate in the governance role? (High / Building / Fragile)

bands.interpretation: Strong governance foundation; credible and effective in board role
Developing capability; some meaningful gaps to address
Significant gaps in board effectiveness; development or honest role assessment required

bands.priority_3: Board exposure expansion (committee leadership, cross-sector mandates)
